title: Draw a flowchart to calculate and print the sum of the first 10 natural numbers (1 to 10). Start, initialize sum = 0 and i = 1, loop while i <= 10 doing sum = sum + i, i = i + 1, print sum, End. Input: none, Expected Output: 55.
shortTitle: Sum of First 10 Numbers — print the sum of 1 to 10

s1_definition.profdef: This computes the sum of the first ten natural numbers by accumulating the counter itself rather than external input. A running total starts at zero and the loop adds each value of the counter from one to ten. The closed-form shortcut, N times N plus one over two, gives the same result in constant time, which for ten is ten times eleven over two equals fifty-five.

The system adds the period numbers one through ten to get fifty-five, or uses the quick formula to get the same answer instantly.
s1_definition.oneliner: The sum of one to N is an accumulation of the counter, and the closed form N times N plus one over two gives it directly without a loop.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This computes the sum of the first ten natural numbers by accumulating the counter itself rather than external input. A running total starts at zero and the loop adds each value of the counter from one to ten. The closed-form shortcut, N times N plus one over two, gives the same result in constant time, which for ten is ten times eleven over two equals fifty-five.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India projects cumulative interest accrual over ten periods where period k contributes k units, so the total accrual is one plus two and so on up to ten. The system adds the period numbers one through ten to get fifty-five, or uses the quick formula to get the same answer instantly.

**One line to remember:** The sum of one to N is an accumulation of the counter, and the closed form N times N plus one over two gives it directly without a loop.

sections.s2_technical:
The loop version seeds a running total at zero and runs a counter from one to ten, adding the counter to the total each step. Unlike the previous problem it does not read external values; the thing being summed is the loop counter itself. After ten iterations the total is fifty-five. The seed is zero for the same identity reason as any sum loop.

The more interesting senior point is the closed-form formula. The sum of the first N natural numbers equals N times N plus one, divided by two. This is Gauss's formula, and it computes the answer in constant time with a single multiplication and division instead of N additions. For ten it is ten times eleven, which is one hundred ten, divided by two, which is fifty-five. In production, if I need the sum of one to N for a large N, I use the formula because it is far faster and avoids any loop overhead.

For money or large counts I would compute the formula with BigInteger or BigDecimal to avoid overflow, since N times N plus one can exceed an int or long for large N. For example `BigInteger.valueOf(n).multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(n + 1)).divide(BigInteger.TWO)` is exact for any N. The division by two is always exact here because N times N plus one is always even, since one of two consecutive integers is even, so there is no rounding concern. A senior nuance is to recognize when a loop can be replaced by a closed form, because that is often the difference between an order-N and a constant-time solution.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India projects a cumulative figure over ten periods where period k contributes k. We must sum one through ten. This is exactly the sum = sum + i accumulation of the counter.

Problem 2 — For large period counts a loop is wasteful when a formula exists. This is exactly why we also provide the closed form N times N plus one over two.

Problem 3 — For large N the intermediate product can overflow a primitive. This is exactly why the formula is computed with BigInteger.

Our mini-project builds a `SeriesSum` with a `sumToN(int n)` loop method and a `sumToNFormula(int n)` closed-form method, and a `SumFirstTenDemo` runnable that shows both give fifty-five for ten.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: none; N is fixed at ten.

Step 1 — The loop method seeds sum to zero and the counter i to one. Nothing has been added yet.

Step 2 — Iteration adds one, making sum one, then two making three, then three making six, then four making ten, continuing upward.

Step 3 — By the time i reaches ten, the running sum has accumulated all the values one through ten, ending at fifty-five, after which i becomes eleven and the loop stops.

Step 4 — The formula method computes ten times eleven, which is one hundred ten, divided by two, which is fifty-five, in a single step with no loop. The division is exact because one hundred ten is even.

Step 5 — Both methods return fifty-five, confirming the loop and the closed form agree, and both results are logged.

Final output:

```
2026-11-01 00:08:00 [INFO] Sum 1..10 via loop    = 55
2026-11-01 00:08:00 [INFO] Sum 1..10 via formula = 55
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The sum of the first ten natural numbers is an accumulation loop where the thing being summed is the loop counter itself. You seed a running total at zero, then add each value of the counter from one to ten, and the result is fifty-five. The seed is zero for the same additive-identity reason as any sum loop.

The more valuable point in an interview is recognizing the closed form. The sum of the first N natural numbers equals N times N plus one, all divided by two, which is Gauss's formula, and it computes the answer in constant time with a single multiplication and division rather than N additions. For ten that is ten times eleven, one hundred ten, divided by two, fifty-five. The division is always exact because N times N plus one is a product of two consecutive integers and therefore always even, so there is no rounding concern. Spotting when a loop can be replaced by a closed form is exactly the kind of optimization that turns an order-N solution into a constant-time one.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this came up in a projection engine where a cumulative figure accrued k units in period k, so the total over N periods was the sum of one to N. I wrote a SeriesSum class offering both a straightforward loop and the closed-form N times N plus one over two, computed with BigInteger so large period counts could not overflow, and I used the formula in production for speed. Both agreed at fifty-five for ten periods. The lesson I carry is that you should always know the closed form for an arithmetic series, because it replaces a loop with a single exact calculation, and using BigInteger keeps it correct no matter how large the count grows.
